name: Chinuk Wawa, Grand Ronde variety
confidence_why: Jacobs 1932, Zenk 1993 and Zenk & Johnson 2004, all from first-hand work, together with Robertson's 2020 tally of the Grand Ronde dictionary, describe stress as fixed word by word with no rule that predicts it (most words initial, French loans final), and the only discrepancy is Grant 2013's survey wording that the default is penultimate rather than initial, which comes to the same thing in the two-syllable words that make up most of the lexicon.

sweep_summary: the list of works with stress in the title for chin1272 holds one title-hit, Edwards 2012 (Language in Society), which is a Seattle Deaf-Blind ethnography and irrelevant (priority none). Beyond the list, the first-hand record for Grand Ronde Chinuk Wawa was read: Zenk 1993 (held by the project) and Zenk & Johnson 2004 (held by the project) state a default of initial stress with item-specific, often variable, non-initial placements (mostly French loans), and Jacobs 1932 (downloaded open from the archive.org scanned of Language vol. 8, saved) states one culminative stress per word fixed per lexical item with no secondary stress and the minimal pair da'nas 'little' / dana's 'little one'. The catalog's lexical coding is confirmed by Jacobs and consistent with Zenk; the catalog's deciding quote from Grant 2013 ('generally penultimate', re-verified on the live APiCS page) is contradicted on the label by the first-hand sources (initial default, 95% per Robertson 2020), so the deciding source should move to Zenk 1993 (+ Jacobs 1932) with Grant kept as secondary and 'penultimate' corrected to 'initial'. Robertson 2018 ('Zenk's Law') adds a claim of trochaic secondary stress citing CTGR 2012 dictionary pp. 380-381, which conflicts with Jacobs' 'no secondary stress'; the 2012 dictionary grammar sketch (print only, priority high) and Zenk's 1984 UO dissertation (ProQuest, priority medium) could not be obtained.org, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, UO Scholars' Bank, the Internet Archive's index).

new_statements.quote: Many items show variable stress-placements and seemingly unmotivated fluctuations of vowel length ... En masse, such items point to a uniform pattern, which may be generalized as follows: In items of CVCV(C).., VCV(C).., or (more unusually) CVCCVC syllable structure, optionally stressed initial syllables occur almost regularly short, while non-initial syllables that may optionally bear stress may also occur long--whether stressed or not ... The patterning of stress in the French-derived portion of the lexicon in particular indicates that items entering the language with non-initial stress tend to develop initially-stressed alternates.
new_statements.citation: Zenk, Henry. 1993. A Basic Chinook Jargon Lexicon. Papers for the 28th International Conference on Salish and Neighbouring Languages (ICSNL 28), pp. 363ff.
new_statements.reading: First-hand Grand Ronde fieldwork by the variety's principal documenter. Stress is fixed per lexical item but variable for many items (initial ~ non-initial alternates), with a language-internal drift toward INITIAL stress; the non-initially stressed stratum is largely French loans with source final stress. Together with Zenk & Johnson 2004 ('usual first-syllable stress accurately characterizes CW') and Jacobs 1932 p. 32 (one culminative stress per word, fixed per item, minimal pair da'nas 'little' vs dana's 'little one', no secondary stress), the first-hand record gives: default initial stress, a lexically specified non-initial set, no computable rule. This keeps the catalog's lexical coding (or, if the catalog allows a default-plus-exceptions class, 'initial, non-strict') but corrects the prose: Grant's 'penultimate' should read 'initial'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule is given: stress is notated entry by entry with an acute mark on the stressed syllable, and the compiler is told that entries without a mark are pronounced with all syllables equally prominent (level stress). In the entries read (pp. 4-30) the marks fall on the first syllable for most Chinook-source items (ty'-ee, waw'-waw, Ma'-mook, Qua'-na-sum, Cuck'qua, Kon'-a-way, E'-lip, Clat'-ta-waw, Em'-na, Chah'-co, Lo'-lo) and on a later, usually final, syllable for French-source items (Le mah', Lahash', La sack', La bot-tee', La chandel', La pe-osh', La-nim') and for some Chinook items (pus-sis'-sey, Ta-man'-ou-is, Cul-li'-ton, A-nah', Ten-as'). A rough regex parse of the scanned (noisy, partial: 37 marked polysyllabic entries caught) gave 14 initial-marked vs 23 non-initial-marked (18 of those final, nearly all French loans); this is an indication of the pattern, not a census of the dictionary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated. Multi-word entries carry one mark per word (e.g. 'Chah'-co yock'-wa', 'ty'-ee pus-sis'-sey'); no secondary-stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Entries printed without an accent mark are to be pronounced with all syllables emphasized alike, i.e. a class of items with no single prominent syllable (47 entries without any mark were caught by the parse; some of these are monosyllables or scanned losses).
new_statements.identity_note: Stuart 1865 describes the Chinook Jargon pidgin in use across Oregon, Washington Territory and British Columbia in the 1860s, compiled by a settler in Montana (published in 'Montana as it is', pp. 103-127); it is an early attestation of the pidgin ancestor of the Grand Ronde creolized variety that chin1272 names, not a description of Grand Ronde speech itself.

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict. All sources (Stuart 1865 marks; Jacobs 1932 p. 32; Zenk 1993; Zenk & Johnson 2004) agree that stress is fixed per lexical item with a Chinook-source stratum stressed mainly on the initial syllable and a French-loan stratum stressed non-initially/finally, with no rule that computes placement. The one tension is Stuart's instruction that unmarked entries be pronounced with 'all the syllables alike' (level stress), versus Jacobs 1932's one culminative stress per word; Stuart was a non-linguist compiling a trade-jargon wordlist, so this is more plausibly a notational convention (he simply did not mark every word) than evidence of a stressless class, and it does not change the reading. Grant's APiCS 'penultimate' remains contradicted by the first-hand sources, as the existing statement already records.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated places ( ll. 446-449, 856-858; opening + tally). (2) The record rests on a 2013 APiCS structural sketch (Grant) whose stress sentence covers Chinuk Wawa generally, plus a 2020 specialist blog tally of the GRCW dictionary; no reference grammar, phonology article or instrumental study of GRCW stress exists (web search: no acoustic/prosody thesis; Glottolog's chin1272 bibliography is mostly mis-attached items). (3) downloaded now via the Internet Archive (UBC live site blocks automated download): Zenk 1993 ICSNL 'A Basic Chinook Jargon Lexicon' — Grand Ronde-only, first-hand — states 'Many items show variable stress-placements', marks optional stress per entry ('chi/'nuk, 'ma/'sachi), and says French-derived final-stressed items 'tend to develop initially-stressed alternates' via 'a phonological process internal

sources.citation: Robertson, David D. 2018-09-15. Zenk's Law. chinookjargon.com (blog).
sources.quote: The average Jargon word has 2 syllables, like English having 'primary' stress on the first one ... Jargon words that are longer than 2 syllables, especially if they have multiples of 2 syllables in them, tend to also have 'secondary' stress every other syllable away from the main stress. Examples would be t'əmánəwàs 'spirit power' and k'ílapày 'come back'. ... I think Henry Zenk is the first to have verbalized our alternating-stresses pattern, for example in an obscure earlier conference paper and on page 380-381 of the Grand Ronde dictionary.
sources.note: Secondary: claims trochaic alternating secondary stress ('Zenk's Law') and cites CTGR 2012 dictionary pp. 380-381 as the primary statement; also reports Jacobs 1932 p. 32 (stressed vs unstressed only). Note the conflict with Jacobs' explicit 'There is no secondary stress'. Points to the print source we lack (see next item).

sources.quote: Only one syllable of a Jargon word receives stress with accompanying high or falling tone. Every independent word or element felt to be an independent word takes stress on that syllable having it regularly. With the stress, higher pitch is always found, quickly falling to normal pitch during or shortly after the articulation of the syllable. Unstressed syllables are uttered in the basic tone of the sentence. There is no secondary stress. Those compounded elements that approach morphologic functioning, such as auxiliary verbs, the demonstrative article u'k, the shorter personal pronouns, ... and even some adjectives, occasionally lose stress.
sources.locator: section STRESS, p. 32; minimal pair p. 31 ('da'nas little; dana's little one'); speaker: Mrs Victoria Howard (Clackamas, Oregon City/Grand Ronde), 'valid only for the Jargon spoken in the northwest Oregon region' (p. 28)
sources.note: Earliest first-hand phonetic description of the Grand Ronde-lineage variety (Victoria Howard). One culminative stress per word, fixed per lexical item ('that syllable having it regularly'), no positional rule given; examples show both initial (ma'muk, ya'rga, da'nas 'little') and final (saya' 'far', dana's 'little one', k!i'labai) stress, including the minimal pair da'nas vs dana's; no secondary stress; clitic/auxiliary elements lose stress; reduplicated disyllables stress and lengthen the second syllable. sources.citation: Zenk, Henry B. & Tony A. Johnson. 2005. Chinookan word classes and Chinuk Wawa etymologies. Papers for ICSNL 40 (UBCWPL), 25 pp.
sources.quote: No general word-stress rule; stress placement in Chinookan source forms decides prefix retention in GRCW nouns ('when the CW form and a closely resemblant Chinookan form both show stress on the n/g prefix, the prefix is retained; when such matching forms show an unstressed n/g prefix, the latter is dropped'). Etymological, silent on the coding.
